answer.exemplar: Simple interest and compound interest differ in what the interest is charged on. Under simple interest the charge each period is a fixed share of the original principal, so the interest earned over the whole time is the principal times the rate times the time, and the balance grows by the same amount every period. The balance under simple interest is therefore a straight line when drawn against time. Under compound interest the charge each period is a share of whatever the balance happens to be at that moment, and the interest is then added to the balance. So the second period charges interest on the original principal plus the first period's interest, the third charges on top of that, and each period earns strictly more than the one before it whenever the rate is positive. That is why the two balances agree exactly after one period and diverge from the second period onwards, and why the gap between them grows faster and faster rather than by a constant amount. Over a long time this is the difference between linear growth and exponential growth, and a five-fold difference over thirty years is entirely ordinary.

questions.explanation: A good answer has to locate the difference in what the interest is charged on rather than just asserting that compounding is different, and it should note that the two agree after a single period, which is what shows the mechanism is interest on interest. A response that stops at the two formulas without explaining the base leaves the reader unable to see why the gap widens. Saying that compounding is always better is too strong, since it depends on the rate and the horizon, and over a single period at a zero rate the two are identical.
questions.hint: Ask what balance each account charges interest on in the second period.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a compounding account and a simple interest account diverge

answer.exemplar: A minimum payment is small by design, and the mechanism that keeps the balance alive is the order in which the payment is used. Interest for the month is charged on the balance at the start of the month, before any payment arrives. If the payment is smaller than that interest, it is entirely absorbed: the interest is collected, and whatever is left over is the only part that reaches the principal. When the payment does not cover the interest, the shortfall is added to the balance, so the next month starts higher, and the interest charged next month is larger too. Each month therefore clears a small slice of the principal while the balance itself stays large enough to keep generating interest, and the interest total can exceed the original purchase price. A borrower who pays more than the minimum, or who pays the whole balance, stops the process: once the payment exceeds the interest, every further dollar comes off the principal, and the balance falls geometrically rather than drifting.

questions.explanation: The reasoning has to identify that interest is charged before the payment and that a payment smaller than the interest leaves the principal untouched, since that is the step the trap depends on. An answer that only says minimum payments are low misses the compounding effect that makes the total interest grow. It should also say what breaks the pattern, otherwise the reader may conclude the balance never falls at all, which is false once payments exceed the interest.
questions.hint: Ask what the payment has to cover first, and when in the month it is charged.
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism behind the minimum payment trap

answer.exemplar: The two percentages describe the same profit, but they are measured against different amounts, and that is the whole of the difference. A markup takes the cost as its base, because the markup is what the seller adds to what it paid, so a cost of 80 dollars marked up by 40 percent means a profit of 32 dollars and a price of 112 dollars. A margin takes the selling price as its base, because the margin is the share of what the customer pays that is profit, so a price of 112 dollars carrying a 40 percent margin would mean a profit of 44.80 dollars, which is not 32. The two coincide only in the degenerate case of a zero profit, where both are zero. Because the price is always larger than the cost for a profitable item, the same profit is always a smaller share of the price than of the cost, so a margin percentage is always lower than the corresponding markup percentage. Quoting a margin as though it were a markup therefore flatters the business, and it is the more common of the two errors because the word margin is used loosely in conversation.

questions.explanation: A strong answer works a single numerical example right through, because the relationship between the two percentages is hard to see symbolically and easy to see in numbers. It should also state the ordering, that the margin is always the smaller of the two for a profitable item, since the price exceeds the cost, and note that the two agree only when there is no profit. An answer that says the two differ without saying which is larger leaves the practical error in place, and one that claims they are interchangeable is worse than no answer.
questions.hint: Pick one cost and one price, and compute both percentages from them.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a margin percentage and a markup percentage are different numbers

answer.exemplar: The advertisement is comparing the two loans on their quoted rates, and the quoted rates are not measuring the same thing. The first loan declares 6 percent a year compounded monthly, so the rate actually charged each period is 0.5 percent, and the balance grows by a factor of 1.005 in each of the twelve months of the year. Over a full year that factor is 1.005 to the twelfth power, which is about 1.0617, so the loan costs about 6.17 percent a year. The second loan declares 6.1 percent a year compounded annually, so it applies its rate once, and it costs exactly 6.1 percent a year. The ranking has therefore reversed: 6.10 percent is below 6.17 percent, so the annually compounded loan is the cheaper of the two even though its quoted rate is higher. The reason is that the first loan's rate is declared on a shorter period, twelve times over, and each of those earlier interest amounts goes on to earn interest of its own. Any comparison of two loans has to be made on effective annual rates, since comparing quoted rates compares different things whenever the compounding frequencies differ.

questions.explanation: The answer must actually compute both effective annual rates, since the reversal only becomes visible once they are placed on one basis, and it should show the monthly rate as 0.5 percent and the twelve factors applied. Saying only that the first is compounded more often is not enough, because that by itself does not establish which is larger. Ending with the general rule that loans must be compared on effective annual rates is what makes the answer useful beyond this pair, and omitting it leaves the reader with a worked example but no principle.
